nodes.id: Subtopic:Environment|Life below water|Ocean research|Coral reef research_qna_001
nodes.label: Science and tech
nodes.question: What is the main focus of the study described in the paragraph?
nodes.answer: The main focus is to assess the heat tolerance of coral populations and its relation to predicting bleaching outcomes during active coral restoration efforts.
nodes.paragraph: Abstract Reef degradation induced by climate change is motivating interest in active management strategies to retain living coral cover including coral restoration. Understand- ing the level and range of heat tolerance available in coral populations is critical to determining their viability and may be important in choosing corals to propagate for restoration projects. There is a need to assess heat tolerance experimen- tally and to relate experimental performance to real-world bleaching conditions and outcomes. We sampled a model population of a key reef-building coral (Montipora capitata ) in K ne ohe Bay, O ahu, Hawai i and subjected fragments to an artificial heat stress profile. We subsequently revisited and assessed source colonies at the height of a natural bleach- ing event. Measurements of photosystem efficiency taken on samples during artificial heat stress were predictive of subsequent field bleaching responses of source colonies. By including experimental performance in additive modeling along with previous measures of symbiont community and source site characteristics, we improved predictions of later field outcomes. Survival of coral samples measured several months after experiencing the heat stress had strong positive predictive value for bleaching outcomes but also produced many false negatives.

Collections In early November 2017, one fragment (~ 20 cm3) was col-lected from each of 5 tagged colonies at each study site to represent the patch reef population. Using genotype assign- ments (Caruso and Rocha de Souza et al. 2022), we detected 5 clonal pairs and one triplet and selected one sample of 401 Coral Reefs (2025) 44:399 409 each to yield a set of unique coral genotypes for final analy - sis. To assess genotype effects, we also collected 25 repli- cate fragments from 8 unique M. capitata genotypes from two previously established study sites (Barott et al. 2021). All fragments were glued on labeled aragonite plugs and acclimated to laboratory conditions for 12 weeks in outdoor seawater tables (Fig. 1B). Experimental temperature profiles We distributed fragments haphazardly into 10 indoor flow- through tanks (40 L) in late January 2018. nodes.question: Why are juvenile COTS difficult to study?
nodes.answer: Juvenile COTS are difficult to study because they are cryptic in the reef infrastructure, making them hard to observe and analyze.
nodes.paragraph: 2023 ; Pratch - ett et al. 2014; Wolfe et al. 2017). The overfishing/preda- tor removal hypothesis posits that adult COTS have been released from predator control (Endean 1969; Kroon et al. 2021). Recent research points to the role that reservoirs of juveniles may have in driving outbreaks, the juveniles-in- waiting hypothesis (Deaker et al. 2020a; Wolfe and Byrne 2024). Given the inherent traits of COTS and plasticity across life stages (Deaker and Byrne 2022), it is likely that many interacting factors across COTS life stages influence outbreaks. Acanthaster begin their benthic life as herbivores. These juveniles are cryptic in the reef infrastructure and are dif- ficult to study (Wilmes et al. 2018, 2020a, b). They feed on crustose coralline algae (CCA) as their preferred food but can subsist on algal films (Deaker et al. 2020b; Lucas 1984 ; Yamaguchi 1973). The juveniles can remain as her - bivores for at least 6.5 years in the absence of coral prey (Deaker et al. 2020a).

nodes.question: What was the main objective of the study outlined in the paragraph?
nodes.answer: The main objective was to understand rates and patterns of symbiont turnover under ambient (non-stressful) conditions in corals.
nodes.paragraph: Abstract The mutualistic relationship between scleractin- ian corals and dinoflagellate algae (Family Symbiodiniaceae) is critical to the success of corals on tropical reefs yet under - pins their vulnerability to climate change. This symbiosis often deteriorates during marine heatwaves as corals rapidly expel their symbionts, inducing mortality unless symbiosis is restored. While symbiont loss during coral bleaching is well-documented, little is known about symbiont turnover and expulsion under non-bleaching environmental condi- tions. To better understand rates and patterns of symbiont turnover under ambient (non-stressful) conditions, we used a novel methodology to capture and quantify expelled sym- bionts of six Caribbean reef-building coral species. Rep- licate 5-cm2 fragments of Acropora cervicornis, Diploria labyrinthiformis, Montastraea cavernosa, Orbicella faveo- lata, Pseudodiploria clivosa and Siderastrea siderea were incubated in 150 mL of 0.2 m filtered seawater and main- tained at 28 C for 7 h during either day (6:0 h 13:0 h) (110 mol quanta m 2 S 1) or night (18:0 h 1:0 h) con- ditions. Seawater from the incubation chambers was then concentrated and symbionts counted using a hemocytometer.

nodes.answer: The main focus is on quantifying diel expulsion rates of symbionts under ambient conditions across various Caribbean reef-building coral species.
nodes.paragraph: 1987; McCloskey et al. 1996; Zhou et al. 2017; Yamashita et al. 2010). Moreover, because expelled symbiont can remain photosynthetically competent after expulsion, they can potentially be reacquired by neighboring adult corals or coral recruits (Ralph et al. 2001; Williamson et al. 2021). However, very little research has explored species-specific variation in ambient expulsion rates or temporal drivers of symbiont regulation (Cui et al. 2023; Yamashita et al. 2010). Research into symbiont expulsion under non-bleaching conditions is vital to better understand symbiont turnover, symbiont community composition, and ambient environmental availability as well as coral-algal symbiosis plasticity and can help us contextualize the effect of thermal stress and bleaching on coral-algal symbiosis. Here we developed a lab-based assay to quantify diel expulsion rates from replicate coral fragments in order to quantify, for the first time, diel patterns of symbiont expulsion under ambient conditions across a variety of Caribbean reef-building coral species. Our results offer insight into the mechanisms driving symbiont turnover and community composition and can inform future work on coral-algal symbiosis during bleaching and subsequent recovery.

nodes.question: What have laboratory studies documented regarding juvenile COTS?
nodes.answer: Laboratory studies have documented their development and transition to a coral diet.
nodes.paragraph: Unless cohorts are monitored from settle - ment, the plasticity of growth in response to environmental conditions complicates the aging of juvenile echinoderms (Byrne et al. 2021). The ontogenetic changes in juvenile COTS from the 5-armed stellate to the multiarmed disk morphology is described in Byrne et al. (2024b). Given their remarkable growth plasticity, a detailed assessment of their growth is needed. To document their development and transition to a coral diet, juvenile COTS have been reared in laboratory studies (Deaker et al. 2020a, b; Johansson et al. 2016; Lucas 1984; Neil et al. 2022; Yamaguchi 1973, 1974). Two of these studies documented growth from metamorphosis through the herbivorous juvenile stage using changes in total diameter and arm number as metrics (Yamaguchi 1973, 1974; Lucas 1984). Yamaguchi (1973) followed the growth of 14 juve- niles for five months and Lucas (1984) documented develop- ment of 6 herbivorous stage juveniles for over a year. nodes.answer: The adults were collected near Cairns, in the northern Great Barrier Reef (GBR).
nodes.paragraph: An ability to age juvenile COTS using morphological traits would greatly enhance our understanding of their biol- ogy and post-settlement processes, as well as the potential of cohorts of juveniles to generate outbreaks. In a model test approach, we addressed the hypothesis that a suite of com- bined traits might be useful to determine the age of COTS juveniles. Using our size-at-age data, we also investigated 703 Coral Reefs (2025) 44:701 719 the fit of growth models to describe age-size relationships of the juveniles. Methods Juvenile rearing As the taxonomy of the Pacific species of Acanthaster is uncertain (Haszprunar et al. 2017 ), we use Acanthaster sp. or COTS to refer to the species investigated here. Adults were collected near Cairns (northern Great Barrier Reef GBR) and shipped to the Sydney Institute of Marine Science where they were maintained in flow-through aquaria supplied with filtered sea water (FSW 5.0 m) at 26 27 C, the sea sur - face temperature of the Northern GBR (AIMS 2023). Small pieces of ovary and testis were dissected from the animals. The ovaries were placed in 10 5 M 1-methyl adenine in FSW to obtain fertile eggs.
